title.narrative: Sustainable Communities for Climate Action in the Yucatán Peninsula (ACCIÓN)

description.narrative:
The overall objective of the Project is to demonstrate an increase in climate resilience of vulnerable populations, ecosystems, and productive systems in the coasts of the Yucatan Peninsula through EbA and sustainable livelihoods.
The specific objectives of the Project are: (i) strengthening the adaptive capacity of communities for coastal and marine ecosystem management and climate change resilience through local EbA solutions, (ii) improving community-based enterprises (CBE) to sustainably manage the natural capital, (iii) channeling private funds to support local EbA solutions and blue carbon projects, and (iv) managing knowledge and promoting coordination with existing public policies.

Figure 4. Theory of change
The Theory of Change (see Figure 4) illustrates that IF marine and coastal ecosystems are conserved and restored, coastal communities’ livelihoods are enhanced, and resilience of vulnerable populations and ecosystems is increased, THEN the ecosystem services that marine and coastal ecosystems provide will be sustained and restored, BECAUSE private investments and financial mechanisms will be aligned and catalyzed to support the restoration, conservation and adapted productive activities through EbA solutions and strengthened community participation.

Component 1: Ecosystem-based adaptation on selected coastal and marine landscapes in the YP
This Component will support the implementation of EbA measures to reduce the vulnerability of the coastal communities and help restore the natural resilience of the region’s coastal and marine ecosystems (see Table 1). The activities supported and approach under this Component are highlighted in the GCF SAP Ecosystems Technical Guidelines. This Component will strengthen the capacities of local communities to adapt to climate change by sustainably managing and conserving their natural resources. The main beneficiaries of this Component will be local coastal communities, who will directly design and implement Sub-projects. This Component will support two financing windows: (i) Funding Window 1. Sub-projects to improve coastal and marine ecosystem management through EbA solutions, and (ii) Funding Window 2: Sub-projects to improve business skills of sustainable community-based enterprises (CBE) and productive groups (PG).
Funding window 1. Sub-projects to improve coastal and marine ecosystem management through EbA solutions.
This Scheme will support the implementation of EbA solutions by local communities. The first year the Project will launch an open and voluntary Request for Proposals (RfP) for Sub-projects (grants) to community-based organizations and productive groups. The Sub-projects will be renewed yearly for up to four years, based on results. The RfP will be focused on EbA solutions that will increase the communities´ adaptive capacity and will have mitigation and socioeconomic co-benefits. The Sub-projects will strengthen communities’ capacities to implement activities related to conservation and restoration of corals, dunes, and blue carbon ecosystems (mangroves and seagrass) (see Table 1 for an example of EbA options and of activities supported by the project and expected impacts for increasing adaptation and reducing vulnerability to climate change).
Sub-projects will be located in approximately ten intervention sites within the selected landscape. The final sites will be defined with funding from the PPF. Potential criteria for selecting sites include: (i) current and future vulnerability to climate change (livelihoods, ecosystems, water), (ii) environmental relevance (for example, Natural Protected Areas, critical ecosystems and Ramsar sites), (iii) existent multi-stakeholder participation and local support, and (iv) information and data availability. The Scheme will support Sub-projects (grants) implemented by the selected organizations. The RfP will prioritize the participation of women, indigenous peoples and the most vulnerable communities. The eligible systems and activities, as well as their potential impact to improve adaptation to climate change is detailed in Table 1. This Component will be linked to the financial mechanism for blue carbon under Component 3, as well to the co-financed parametric insurance for coral reefs under Component 2.
Funding window 2. Sub-projects to improve business skills and diversification of ecosystem-based livelihoods of sustainable community-based enterprises (CBE) and productive groups (PG).
This Scheme will strengthen capacities of CBEs and PGs working on/transitioning to sustainable ecosystem-based livelihoods, including small-scale fisheries, aquaculture, organic apiculture and sustainable tourism. These sectors are key in the region and highly vulnerable to climate (see Table 1). The final sectors will be defined during the PPF process. The Project will provide technical assistance to improve their internal organization and business management skills to increase their profitability and develop financial inclusion, while sustainably managing or conserving the natural capital of YP coastal and marine landscape.
The Project will open a voluntary RfP to Local Providers of Technical Assistance (PLATs, for its acronym in Spanish), which may be civil society organizations, independent consultants or consulting firms. A strong gender approach will be part of this process, informed by the Gender Analysis, and including specific actions from the design of the RfP, selection, and implementation. The PLATs will submit a proposal to improve business skills of sustainable CBE and PG for four years. Once the proposals are selected, the PLAT will undertake an initial assessment of the internal capacity building needs of the CBE and PG, and will design a tailored four-year technical assistance plan addressing themes such as internal organization and governance, business vision, accounting, creditworthiness, marketing, among others. If necessary, specialized consultants could complement the PLATs on specific technical and business needs. For those CBE and PG that have the capacities to access to credits, the EE will link them to relevant credit lines and the PLATs will support them in the process of obtaining and repaying these credits.
Selected CBE and PG may leverage the skills gained through the Project to access other sources of financial resources, including “credits for results” and other private parallel financing under Component 2. Additionally, in case of a climatic event, the CBEs and PGs supported under this Component may be eligible of the Community Emergency Fund supported by Component 2 and linked to the co-financed parametric insurance.
Output 1.1: Improved coastal and marine ecosystem management through EbA solutions.
Activities:
1.1.1 Finance Sub-projects to implement EbA solutions to improve coastal and marine management.
Output 1.2: Improved business skills of sustainable community-based enterprises (CBE) and productive groups (PG).
Activities
1.2.1 Finance Sub-projects to strengthen the capacities of CBE and PG working on/transitioning to sustainable agriculture, small scale fisheries, aquaculture, organic apiculture and sustainable tourism.
Component 2: Sustainable financing for scaling up EbA projects
This Component builds on Component 1 and seeks to mobilize financing to scale-up activities implemented at community level. The project will be catalizing private sector opportunities and will align private investments to strengthen and scale-up the Sub-projects that are ready to manage this type of investment. FMCN will identify investments that seek to reduce vulnerability to promote coordination activities and will promote coordination with national and international initiatives to align finance (see Annex 5). The EE will engage the private sector (including tourism/hotels) to promote and scale-up EbA solutions based on lessons learned. Connecting the Mesoamerican Reef region initiatives with the Climate Initiative in the YP and the national coastal and marine projects being promoted countrywide creates an opportunity to scaling up the EbA solutions promoted by this Project.
This Component will implement two main strategies: (i) design and implement a “credit for results” scheme, and (ii) implement a Community Emergency Fund linked to the co-financed coral reef parametric insurance.
The “credit for results” scheme to upscale ecosystem-based livelihoods. It will be an innovative blended finance tool that will mobilize private finance by delivering risk-adjusted returns. The project will first promote the transition and technical assistance grants to EbA Sub-projects (through Component 1), second will provide a grant (in the form of first-loss capital or other schemes to be evaluated in the PPF) to provide differentiated interest rates and credit structures subordinated to the expected impact in resilience (Component 2), and third, will attract impact investors to provide capital on this financial structure. The expected impact in resilience will be evaluated through a taxonomy developed in the PPF. This type of “credit for results” have proven to be effective for other sectors in Mexico (credits for small businesses with gender lens, financing businesses with the inclusion of vulnerable groups). Investors are interested to profide funding, and financial institutions are interested in implementing this scheme by providing credits from their sources but require partners to offer blended grants and technical assistance to support the transition.. The credits for results will be provided to beneficiaries of Component 1, as well as other CBEs and PGs working on/transitioning to sustainable ecosystem-based livelihoods, including, sustainable agriculture, small scale fisheries, aquaculture, organic apiculture and sustainable tourism.
The Community Emergency Fund linked to the co-financed coral reef parametric insurance. The co-finance from this project will be provided by the the Reef Rescue Initiative (RRI) including the coral reef parametric insurance, which is coordinated by the Mesoamerican Reef Fund (MAR Fund). Parametric reef insurance is an innovative financial mechanism that will cover the costs of rapid response actions to identify and address damage to reefs after the impact of a hurricane. The State of Quintana Roo, Mexico, became the first to pay for parametric insurance for reefs against hurricanes for the Cancun and Puerto Morelos’s reefs, promoted by The Nature Conservancy. The new parametric insurance takes the lessons learned and expands the insurance in two other sites in the Yucatan Peninsula. This innovative financial mechanism will provide predictable, timely funds for rapid response reef restoration in the wake of damaging hurricanes. The project partners are MAR Fund, Willis Towers Watson, and Ocean Risk and Resilience Action Alliance (ORRAA). They have been working with local governments and stakeholders to design and deploy parametric insurance products in two sites in Mexico, starting 2023. When the insurance is triggered, the funding will finance activities to restore coral reefs.
The GCF funding will complement this co-finance, by implementing a Climatic Emergency Fund explicitly devoted for CBEs and PGs whose livelihoods are also affected by the climatic events that triggers the parametric insurance. The Emergency Fund will ensure rapid and effective response to climatic emergencies that affect the CBEs and PGs, who do not directly receive the funding from the parametric insurance but are also affected by the event. The funding will be rapidly disbursed by a flexible RfP that will open once the parametric insurance is activated. For the potential investors and financial institutions, the Climatic Emergency Fund will be seen as a de-risking mechanism in case of climatic events, ensuring that the business will continue operation and will be able to pay the credit in case of a climatic event.
The FMCN has successful experiences in implementing Emergency Funds in case of fires and other emergencies, and will replicate the experience with CBEs and PGs.
Output 2.1: Increased impact investment to scale-up EbA solutions in the YP.
Activities:
2.1.1 Catalyze and align private investments for scaling-up EbA Sub-projects.
2.1.2 Design and implement a “credit for results” scheme for scaling-up EbA Sub-projects and CBE under Component 1.
Output 2.2: Implemented Community Emergency Fund linked to the co-financed coral reef parametric insurance.
Activities:
2.1.3 Implement a coral reef parametric insurance (co-financed).
2.1.4 Implement a Climatic Emergency Fund linked to the co-financed coral reef parametric insurance to finance community-based Sub-projects affected by climatic events.
Component 3. Financial mechanism for conservation and restoration of mangroves (blue carbon)
The Project will implement a financial mechanism for blue carbon projects for conservation, restoration and improved management of mangroves and seagrass. The benefited communities will be those with land covered with mangroves supported under Component 1 and other coastal communities interested to participate in the mechanism.
This Component will be built on FMCN technical expertise, solid reputation, and capacity to link a variety of actors -from local communities to international corporations- to accelerate the implementation of the blue carbon financial mechanism. The financial mechanism will be designed under the PPF and will allow to increase financial resources to the local communities for the conservation and restoration of their blue carbon ecosystems, generating climatic, environmental and social benefits, including the diversification of income. At local level, the Project will increase the community´s resilient capacity and will have mitigation co-benefits for both men and women. The Component will work with companies´ and individuals to link them to community blue carbon credits from the voluntary market. The financial mechanisms will incorporate and scale lessons learned from existent initiatives, such as the Mexican Alliance of Blue Carbon (of which FMCN is one of the 6 members). The valuation of ecosystem services will serve as a basis to raise awareness of the value of the services provided by coral reefs, mangroves, and seagrass.
The promoted blue carbon initiatives will be linked to the country's advances in this area. Additionally, lessons learned from the voluntary credit schemes promoted by this Project will inform the national Blue Carbon strategies (under development), led by the Ministry of Environment (SEMARNAT). Additionally, we are currently under discussion with the private sector to explore under PPF the possibility of a “blue carbon accelerator program”.
Output 3.1: Established financial mechanism for blue carbon.
Activities:
3.1.1 Design and establish a financial mechanism for the conservation and restoration of mangroves and implementation of blue carbon projects.
3.1.2 Implement ecosystem services quantification and valuation for coral reefs, mangroves and seagrass.
3.1.3 Promote blue carbon voluntary credits by linking individuals and companies with blue carbon projects to compensate their emissions.
Component 4: Knowledge management and coordination with existing public policies
A critical gap in the YP coastal and marine landscape is the lack of knowledge on the available options to integrate EbA within natural resource management. At the local level, people are aware of the increasing climatic variability that is negatively affecting their livelihoods. However, they need to strengthen the understanding of the connection between the impacts of climate change, the importance of ecosystem integrity and the link between this and their economic activities. The Project will have a strong learning and knowledge management Component to capture and disseminate lessons learned and to influence policy. The knowledge generated through this Project will be shared with regional and local level institutions such as the Yucatan Peninsula Regional Commission on Climate Change, which can provide lessons to guide the other regions in Mexico.
The lessons learned will be shared through various appropriate local and regional networks. The Project will strengthen existent regional initiatives that promote cross-cutting strategies in various sectors and at different levels to implement policies with EbA approaches. Information on the Project will be produced and disseminated among government authorities, technical and financial partners and beneficiaries. Moreover, a local database will be created to collect and process, preserve and disseminate datasheets, educational tools and other training materials for their replication.
The Project will strengthen local instruments in two sectors with critical climatic risks that could contribute to the adaptation to climate change and food security (see section B.1.): (i) small-scale fisheries, and (ii) mangrove conservation and restoration, as a measure that contributes to adaptation and mitigation of climate change at a regional scale.
Strengthen local instruments related to small-scale fisheries. The Project will strengthen the Kanan Kay Alliance (AKK for its Spanish acronym). AKK is an initiative of a network of 34 organizations, including the largest fishing cooperatives of the region, that have established fish replenishment zones. AKK seeks the recovery of small-scale fisheries and the protection of coastal marine ecosystems through organized efforts to make more efficient use of resources. This initiative began in Quintana Roo in 2010, and it has protected more than 19,000 hectares, making it a reference at the regional level. Time is ripe to expand AKK through the Yucatan Peninsula, as its strategic plan 2020-2025 considers. The Project will strengthen AKK by facilitating collaborative processes and shared actions of responsible fisheries management (fish replenishment zones in the three states of the YP) to recover the productivity of artisanal fisheries through virtual and in-person Assemblies and capacity building of fishers.
Strengthen local instruments related to blue carbon. The Project will strengthen the regional blue carbon initiatives, to mitigate and adapt to climate change, based on the conservation and restoration of the YP mangroves. It channels private resources to communities in the field that implement conservation, restoration and monitoring activities and supports the transition to climate-resilient rural livelihoods. The Project will share lessons learned from Component 3 and will promote spaces for regional coordination, and capacity building of members representing different stakeholders, to enhance opportunities for climate change mitigation and adaptation based on blue carbon ecosystems. Annex 5 shows the initiatives that the Project will coordinate through this Component.
Design and improve local hydrometeorological early warning system. This Project will scale-up the use of existing online Early Warning Systems (EWS) for fires and hydrometeorological events through capacity building to small producers, ejidos, academia, NGOs, and private companies located in the selected areas of ACCIÓN to notify in suitable platforms (specific apps, SMS, WhatsApp, Facebook, Twitter, local radio, among others). This system will be built on different initiatives in the region that are not currently coordinated and will support vulnerable communities in their planning, saving their life, property and protecting their climate resilient-rural livelihoods. The information generated by this system will complement the algorithm of the co-financed parametric insurance to activate the CBE emergency fund for CBE.
Output 4.1: Enhanced effective knowledge management to inform decision-making at all levels.
Activities:
4.1.1 Implement a communication strategy and appropriate knowledge products, to share results and lessons learned.
4.1.2 Conduct knowledge-exchange activities and local level forums and scale-up into state, regional, and national level policies.
Output 4.2: Strengthened local instruments and regional mechanisms that contribute in reducing climate change vulnerability.
Activities:
4.2.1 Strengthen and upscaling small-scale fisheries initiative by supporting its operation, consolidation and promoting spaces for regional coordination.
4.2.2 Strengthen the coordination of existing blue carbon regional initiatives by sharing lessons learned and promoting spaces for regional coordination.
4.2.3 Design and improve an online hydrometeorological early warning system and establish a fire prevention and control mechanism.

Potential for transformation and scaling-up. The lessons learned from Components 1 and 3 will be shared with the national authorities through the leadership of the Project staff housed at CONANP, to ensure the incorporation of this new knowledge into the national carbon strategies. Under Component 4, the Project will ensure coordination with other public and private initiatives in the region, and will provide lessons learned to be scaled-up into state, regional and national programs. Under Component 4, and by supporting local governments, the project will adapt at subnational level the progress of the national blue carbon strategy.
The Project will also serve as a basis for the Climate Action and Blue Finance Project for the Mesoamerican Reef Region, which is currently under design and is expected to be financed by the GCF (over $30M to be submitted in late 2021 by IUCN). The lessons learned of ACCIÓN will be scaled-up in the Mesoamerican Region.
Exit Strategy. This Project is organically designed to scale-up outcomes sequentially, from the implementation of local Sub-projects and local development of capacities (Component 1), long-term financial sustainability through financial mechanisms (Component 2 and Component 3), and coordination at the regional and national levels (Component 4). Systematically mainstreaming local adaptation approaches into local, regional and national planning processes is usually the best way to support the wide-scale replication of local approaches and achieve impact at scale. As part of the exit strategy of the proposed GCF Project, activities will focus on developing a regional EbA upscaling strategy and generating policy recommendations to support the sustained replication of the Project’s activities beyond the implementation period. Opportunities for mainstreaming EbA into regional development planning will include implementing activities in concordance with the National NDC, NPA climate change adaptation programs, municipal adaptation programs and ecological zoning plans with criteria for climate change adaptation, and support for regional blue carbon initiatives. Through this EbA upscaling strategy, aligned with the Project’s policy recommendations, the Project will identify public, private and bilateral sources of funding to address financing gaps through Components 2 and 3.
Implementation arrangements. The proposed Implementation arrangements are similar to the scheme implemented by the C6 Project, implemented by FMCN with funding from GEF. The arrangements were recognized by the World Bank as an efficient and cost-effective practice.
The accredited entity (AE) is the Mexican Fund for the Conservation of Nature (FMCN), which has a strong structure and capacities for the implementation of multilateral-financed projects. For example, FMCN recently concluded the implementation of the “Coastal watersheds conservation in the context of climate change” (C6), GEF-financed for USD$39.5 million. All Project goals were met, and it has been recognized as a best practice by GEF for its inter-institutional collaboration. FMCN has the adequate capacity to carry out the administration and supervision of the Project, given its trajectory in implementing projects financed by international institutions such as the World Bank, the State Development Bank of the Federal Republic of Germany (KfW) and the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), among others. FMCN's internal control is solid, since it has manuals, policies and operating procedures that will be applicable to the execution of the Project.
The Executing Entities is the FMCN and a Regional Fund (RF), Sureste Sostenible. This RF is one of the six funds created by FMCN in the past seven years. The use of RF for Project execution has proved to reduce operation costs by working closer to the community-based enterprises and local organizations, developing capacities to finance projects, strengthening partners in the field, joining efforts by creating programs, and strengthening coalitions. Together, these six RFs and FMCN are part of the Mexican Network of Environmental Funds or RedFAM. The due diligence and capacity assessment of the Regional Fund will be carried out as part of the PPF. Table 2 shows the activities and sub activities that will be responsible of each EE.
The Coordination Committee (CC) will be composed primarily by national and state government authorities, and climate change experts and practitioners. The CC will provide guidance, ensuring alignment with the regional perspective in achieving both resilient ecosystems and coastal communities. The CC will also design the RfP for Sub-projects and PLATs.
CONANP, the federal agency in charge managing Natural Protected Areas, will provide key technical inputs during Project implementation in protected areas, and will ensure coordination with national government, promoteing scaling-up the local strategies and lessons learned

FMCN (AE and EE) through Sureste Sostenible (EE) will disburse financial resources to the PLATs to improve the business skills of sustainable CBE and PG under the supervision of Sureste Sostenible. FMCN and Sureste Sostenible will coordinate with CONANP activities in Natural Protected Areas. Risk assessment and management. The Project has identified three main risk factors to consider. The first is related to rural community engagement not being accomplished limiting the adoption of restoration activities and climate-resilient rural livelihoods. The diversity of peoples, knowledge, and contexts found in the YP requires tailored, place-based strategies to involve indigenous and non-indigenous communities in developing adequate adaptation measures that shall be sustained over time. The mitigation measure will focus on building on existing networks, consultation, awareness-raising, and capacity building processes to address the concerns, opinions, and visions from potential beneficiaries and other relevant stakeholders affected by the Project as part of a participatory decision-making practice. Therefore, the proposed interventions will be culturally appropriate, as well as supported and endorsed by the communities, encouraging their participation and empowerment. The second risk refers to coordination difficulties with public and private institutions that may decrease the alignment of activities, investments, and policies to foster and scale-up climate-resilient rural livelihoods. The Project will foster cross-sectoral collaboration arrangements with several governmental agencies to foster the alignment of federal, state, and municipal investments and policies. The Project will also strengthen rural organizations of sustainable producers to access better market opportunities and prices. The third risk factor is related to the vulnerability of the Yucatan Peninsula to the impacts of extreme hydro meteorological events. The mitigation measure includes the development of an early warning system for community use, as well as planning on-the-ground activities from November to April when the risk of extreme weather events is significantly lower. Additional co-financing will be granted to ensure that climate risk is considered and mitigation measures implemented in the selected Sub-projects. The main Project risks are described in Annex 3 and 4.
Monitoring and evaluation. FMCN will be responsible for Project monitoring and will provide oversight of the RF involved in developing capacities in local organizations for Component 1. Progress will be measured against the Results Framework. The Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) plan will include the midterm and final independent evaluations. The final review will assess the achievement of indicators, sustainability of results, and identify lessons learned. A key part of the Project is the participatory nature of the M&E, to serve as a tool to empower beneficiaries to improve the management of their resources, and to ensure long-term sustainability. The academic sector will play a key role in M&E.
